What individual therapy is

More than talking. More than being given advice.

Individual psychotherapy is a one-to-one process for understanding difficulties and working toward changes in thoughts, emotions, behavior, or daily functioning. Different approaches organize that work differently. A clinician may focus on present-day patterns, coping, relationships, or a combination that fits the concerns being assessed.

The starting question is not simply what is wrong. It is what is happening, how it affects your life, what you have already tried, and what a useful change would look like. A therapy plan gives the conversations a direction without requiring you to know every answer at the first appointment.

For example, wanting more confidence can become something more recognizable: speaking in a meeting without rehearsing for an hour, making a decision without repeatedly seeking reassurance, or expressing a limit without abandoning it immediately. These are illustrative goals, not promises or a prescribed list of outcomes.

Sources psychotherapy

Your priorities belong here

You are not a project to be fixed.

You bring knowledge of your own life. A clinician brings a way to assess concerns, notice patterns, and help organize the work. Collaboration means there is room to question an interpretation, discuss a technique, or say that a goal no longer fits.

You do not have to make your story sound tidy to deserve attention. A useful beginning might be: I am keeping up, but it is taking much more out of me than anyone sees.

A process with room to adapt

How the work can take shape.

A possible sequence, not a fixed curriculum or a promise that every clinician works identically.

01

Understand the situation

The first clinical conversation gathers context: the reason for seeking help, relevant history, current functioning, and safety or health concerns. An assessment helps identify what needs attention before a plan is chosen. You can ask what a question is for and explain when something is difficult to discuss.

02

Make the goal usable

A broad concern becomes a shared focus. Instead of only saying less stress, you might discuss what you want to be able to do when stress appears. The difference matters: a goal should connect the appointments to your life, not simply describe how you wish you felt.

03

Try, notice, and revisit

Depending on the approach, work can include reflection, practicing a conversation, noticing patterns, or trying a manageable action between sessions. Later conversations examine what happened, what remains hard, and whether the plan needs to change. A difficult week is information, not a grade.

Sources psychotherapy prepare

A closer look

From a vague hope to a specific direction.

The same concern can lead to very different work. Here is one way a goal could become clearer.

Fictional teaching example. Not a diagnosis, a client story, or an assigned exercise.

01

The starting concern

A fictional adult says, I need to stop being so overwhelmed. Their week contains deadlines, family requests, and little time to recover. They are not sure which part belongs in therapy.

02

The pattern to examine

In the example, saying yes brings immediate relief from disappointing someone. Later, the extra commitment creates resentment and exhaustion. That sequence is more specific than simply being bad at boundaries.

03

A possible direction

The conversation could focus on recognizing the pressure to agree, making room to consider a request, and communicating an honest limit. It could also include the practical reality that some responsibilities cannot simply be removed.

What would count as useful change in this example?

Not a life without obligations. A more useful marker might be noticing a request before automatically accepting it, discussing an alternative, or recognizing when additional practical support is needed. The goal is defined together and can change as more is understood.

This is a teaching example, not an account of a client or a claim about what treatment will achieve. It shows why a personal goal needs more detail than a symptom label.

Understanding the options

A service and an approach are different things.

Individual therapy describes the setting.

It means you are the person attending the work with a clinician. It does not tell you whether sessions will be highly structured, reflective, focused on relationships, or a blend. You can discuss family or relationship concerns without every person in the story attending.

Couples and family services involve different arrangements. Explore services when the question is who should participate. This page does not determine which service is appropriate for your situation.

An approach describes how the work is organized.

Cognitive behavioral therapy examines links among situations, interpretations, feelings, and actions. Other approaches may emphasize different aspects of experience. A method name is useful when it leads to an explanation of what you would actually do, not just an acronym in a biography.

Different methods can be integrated, but their purpose should remain understandable. Compare therapy approaches for orientation, then discuss how the clinician would connect a method to your goals.

Sources nhs-cbt

A practical choice

Woodinville or online: make room to participate.

In the Woodinville office

Consider travel time, accessibility, and the transition into and out of an appointment. An office can give the conversation a dedicated place away from household activity. M.F.T. has one physical office; the community pages elsewhere on this site do not represent additional branches.

View the office details before planning a visit.

Online in an eligible location

A private setting, reliable audio and connection, and a plan for interruptions matter more than simply having a video link. Tell the clinician where you will physically be, including when traveling, and confirm eligibility. Do not attend while driving.

Explore Washington online care. Availability and suitability depend on the clinician and the situation.

Questions before you begin

The things you may be wondering.

Do I need a diagnosis before I contact you?

No diagnosis is needed to ask about care. The first clinical assessment is where a clinician can explore the concern and whether a diagnosis is supported. That is separate from whether a service can be billed to insurance. Coverage and medical necessity need their own review; a free introduction does not establish them.

What should I bring to a first appointment?

A short starting note can be enough: what led you to book, how it is affecting daily life, and what you hope to understand. Relevant health information, medications, previous treatment, and questions can also be useful. Use the approved intake process for private information, not this public website or an advertising link.

Sources prepare

Will every session involve homework?

Not every approach or appointment uses the same kind of between-session work. CBT often includes agreed practice. Other work may involve reflection, noticing something in daily life, or no assigned activity. A useful task has a purpose you understand and an arrangement you can discuss, rather than being an unexplained test of commitment.

Sources nhs-cbt

How will I know whether therapy is helping?

Agree on what you want to notice outside appointments, and revisit it. A fictional goal of communicating a limit is more concrete than becoming a better person. Discuss both what is changing and what is not. There is no universal session count or guaranteed outcome on this page; the plan and its usefulness need ongoing review.

Can I talk about a relationship on my own?

Yes, the concerns you bring may involve relationships even when you attend individually. Individual work does not let a clinician assess an absent partner or decide their motives from one account. When the intended work requires more participants, the service and privacy arrangements should be clarified rather than assuming an individual visit becomes couples care.

How do I check what I will pay?

Use Verify benefits to start an inquiry about individual services. Ask how to provide the needed information safely; leave insurance numbers and clinical details out of the initial email. Confirm the fee for private-pay care. Verification is not a promise that an insurer will pay.

Still have a practical question? Email the support team.
